extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys, patent agents and practitioners drafting patent claims (international practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for drafting patent claims (formatting, wording, claim types, and claim sets) across multiple jurisdictions, with practical examples and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripheral claiming doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Most countries follow a 'peripheral claiming' doctrine in which the claims establish the outer limits of patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to set the limits of the scope of protection sought. Do not assume a 'central claiming' approach unless filing in a rare jurisdiction that uses it. Claims should be written with examiners, courts and potential licensees in mind so the intended boundaries are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plain language (the vs said)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the words 'the' and 'said' are interchangeable in claims drafting (e.g., 'the pencil' or 'said pencil'), the latter is increasingly old-fashioned and jurisdictions trend toward plain language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain language over legalese (avoid 'said' where unnecessary), especially if litigation in jurisdictions (e.g., U.S.) may involve lay juries. Use wording that aids comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and formatting of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For clarity, claims are frequently more extensively punctuated than grammatically required: a comma typically separates the preamble from the transitional phrase; a colon typically separates the transition from the body; the body is often broken into small paragraphs with elements separated by semi-colons and the penultimate element followed by '; and,' the last ending with a full stop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the model: Preamble, transitional phrase: – Element (#1); – Element (#2); and – Element (#3). In some countries (e.g., U.S.) each element or combination should be indented on its own line; in others indentation is optional. Use punctuation to ensure the claim will be interpreted as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements in a patent claim must demonstrate correct antecedent basis: introduce an element with 'a' or 'an' on first use and refer back to it with 'the' thereafter; each new claim set must re-establish antecedent basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide correct antecedent basis may cause ambiguity (e.g., whether 'the pencil' refers to the same pencil). To refer to multiple instances, use 'first' and 'second' or 'an' and 'another'. Draft each claim independently and re-introduce elements in each new claim set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference numerals and parenthetical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions (PCT) prefer reference numerals in parentheses after claim elements to link claims to drawings; many countries state numerals shall not be interpreted as limiting the claims; some jurisdictions avoid or prohibit numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reference numerals where encouraged to support comprehension, but be aware that (i) adding substantive text inside parentheses may create 'special features' and be interpreted as limiting, (ii) some offices may reject parenthetical expressions without numerals (e.g., '(concrete) molded brick'), and (iii) inclusion of numerals does not incorporate the drawings into the claim. If filing in jurisdictions (e.g., U.S.) that discourage numerals, avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and use of claim phrases ('wherein', 'whereby', etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words have special meanings in claims: words such as 'wherein', 'whereby', 'such that', 'so as to', and 'configured to' are used to further define structure or provide a function associated with a structure; a 'wherein clause' is generally used to describe a function, operation or result that flows from the previously recited structure or function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know how courts/examiners in relevant jurisdictions interpret these phrases and use them appropriately. Use 'wherein' when the result necessarily follows from the recited structure or function; consider effects on claim scope and dependency when choosing phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for multiple elements (avoid single-element claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices require claims to recite at least two elements; a single-element claim can be impossibly broad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting trivially broad single-element claims (e.g., 'A computer, comprising: a processor.') which may read on prior art or trivial items. Include enough limitations to meaningfully define the invention's scope relative to the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part (improvement / Jepson) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-part claim (also called an improvement or Jepson claim) sets out the most relevant known prior art in the preamble, uses a transitional phrase (e.g., 'characterized by'/'characterized in that' or 'wherein the improvement comprises'), and the body characterizes the improvement (the novel elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the two-part format constitutes an implicit admission that the first part is prior art. The EPO prefers two-part claims where appropriate and advises that the first part should indicate the technical class and prior-art features necessary for definition. Consider whether the two-part form is appropriate—it's often unsuitable for inventions that are combinations of known integers of equal status, certain process modifications, complex interrelated systems, or new chemical compounds. You may initially draft standard format claims and switch if required by an examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative elements and Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jurisdictions allow alternative elements in a single claim; expressions such as 'metal or plastic' can be ambiguous in claims. Markush claim format ('wherein element A is selected from the group consisting of X, Y and Z') is commonly used (especially in chemistry) to claim alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'and/or' or explicit phrasing ('selected from the group consisting of...') where inclusive alternatives are meant; use 'either ... or ...' for exclusive alternatives. If combinations of members are possible, explicitly say so (e.g., 'and combinations thereof'). Markush groups must not be ambiguous; if one alternative is anticipated by prior art, the entire Markush claim may lack novelty—consider separate dependent claims for group members and ensure unity of invention requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional elements and means-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language can define a claim element by what it accomplishes rather than by what it is. Means-plus-function claims use the word 'means' followed by a function and are interpreted variably across jurisdictions—often limited to the structures disclosed in the specification and their equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functional element is acceptable so long as a person skilled in the art can perform the function without inventive skill. Means-plus-function claims typically must be supported by adequate disclosure of structures in the specification; explicitly describe structures that perform recited functions (e.g., 'tapes, adhesives, rivets') to avoid overly narrow constructions. Avoid reciting unnecessary structures or failing to identify which structures perform the function. Beware that wholly functional claim sets risk rejection as mere desiderata (desired result without how to achieve it). Mixing means-plus-function and structural claim elements is possible and often desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim sets: independent and dependent claims (scope, fees, balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification normally contains one or more independent claims and several dependent claims. All applications must contain at least one independent claim directed to the essential features necessary to satisfy legal patentability requirements (e.g., novelty, inventive step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a balanced set of claims (broad and narrow) to protect different aspects and levels of detail. Consider costs: many offices levy filing/examination/grant fees based on claim counts (and extra fees for multiple dependent claims in some offices like the USPTO). Avoid both overly broad and overly narrow claims; ensure claims are clear and reasonable in number relative to the invention's complexity. Dependent claims inherit all features of their parent claim and are always narrower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claims characteristics and unity of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims represent the broadest claims and stand alone; multiple independent claims may be needed to cover different aspects. Unity of invention requires that multiple independent claims in one application relate to one invention or a group of inventions linked as a single general inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare several independent claims when the invention encompasses different aspects or when strategically varying breadth is useful to hedge against unknown prior art. Be mindful of jurisdictional limits on the number/kind of independent claims (e.g., EPO limits independent claims per category). Ensure independent claims include essential features for the technical effect and comply with unity requirements to avoid objections or divisionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims formatting and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim refers back to a preceding claim and includes all features of that claim even if not repeated; dependent claims make the text more concise and are inherently narrower than the claim they depend on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal dependencies clearly (e.g., 'The apparatus of Claim 1, further comprising...'). Use dependent claims to capture fallback positions and specific embodiments. Remember that some offices charge additional fees for multiple dependent claim forms and that dependent claims should be reasonable in number and clear in scope.
